items.title: A Global Rebound for Mangroves
items.short_description: After decades of decline, this ecologically significant type of forest is making a comeback.
items.abstract: After decades of decline, this ecologically significant type of forest is making a comeback. For decades, the story they told about mangroves was dominated by loss and decline. A global rebound began around 2010, the scientists found, led by the expansion of mangrove forests in Asia, Australia, and South America. The country lost mangroves rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s due to the expansion of agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting in coastal areas, but the trend reversed around 2010, when mangrove area began expanding in many places. The pair of Landsat images above shows expansion of mangrove forests in Palaw Township in Burma's Myeik District—an area that has seen both significant regeneration of degraded mangrove forests and the spread of trees into new areas since 2010.

items.title: Scotland’s Flow Country
items.short_description: Blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands store vast amounts of carbon.
items.abstract: Blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands store vast amounts of carbon. Compared to ecosystems in many other parts of the world, the blanket bogs of the Flow Country in northern Scotland are unassuming—soggy, treeless landscapes dominated by hummocky mosses, grasses, and heathers. The image above, captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8, is centered on blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands, home to the largest such ecosystem in Europe. Some parts of the Flow Country have been accumulating peat for more than 9,000 years, building deposits exceeding eight meters thick, according to UNESCO. Overall, scientists estimate that all of the world’s peatlands cover just 3 percent of Earth’s land surface but store more than 600 gigatons of carbon—about twice as much as all the world’s forests combined.

items.title: Water Surges Into Navajo Reservoir
items.short_description: Rounds of heavy rain in the U.S. Southwest flooded rivers and rapidly raised New Mexico’s second-largest reservoir.
items.abstract: Rounds of heavy rain in the U.S. Southwest flooded rivers and rapidly raised New Mexico’s second-largest reservoir. Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest in late October and early November 2026. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods. One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks.

items.title: Autumn Mornings Bring Valley Fog
items.short_description: Low clouds trace the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River, then burn off by afternoon.
items.abstract: Low clouds trace the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River, then burn off by afternoon. On a cool November morning, low clouds traced the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River. The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-21 acquired the right image that afternoon, after the clouds had dissipated and exposed the rivers and lakes beneath them. Notice the fog filling the branching valleys across part of the Appalachian Plateau in eastern Kentucky and southwestern West Virginia. The same pattern is visible along the Cumberland River and its reservoirs in north-central Tennessee and south-central Kentucky. According to the National Weather Service, temperatures in many places on the morning of November 8 dipped into the 30s Fahrenheit before giving way to a mild, sunny afternoon.

items.title: Ozone Hole Reaches Its 2026 Maximum
items.short_description: The ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring, but it was not as deep as other large holes on record.
items.abstract: The ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring, but it was not as deep as other large holes on record. The data visualizations below show the ozone hole each year from 1979 through 2026 (no data are available for 1995). Records in depth and area have never occurred in the same year (the largest ozone hole occurred in 2006), but the long-term trend in both characteristics is consistent: from 1980 through the early 1990s, the hole rapidly grew in area and depth. Measured by its mean size from September 7 to October 13, which is peak ozone depletion season, the 2026 hole was the seventh largest in 48 years of monitoring. The map at the top of this page shows the hole on September 18, the day of its annual maximum area.

items.title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
items.short_description: The San Juan River has carved deep, improbably curvy meanders into the desert landscape.
items.abstract: The San Juan River has carved deep, improbably curvy meanders into the desert landscape. Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today's Mississippi River. In a bygone geologic era, the San Juan flowed across a relatively flat plain that formed in an ancient marine environment. Today, on its westward path to Lake Powell, the San Juan River flows through an impressive series of entrenched meanders, also known as “goosenecks.” An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the stark desert topography on October 6, 2026. In Utah’s Goosenecks State Park, the river runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep. One section is so curvy that the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 kilometers) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 kilometers) apart as the crow—nay, goose—flies.

items.title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites
items.short_description: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea exposes an ancient piece of the ocean floor and hosts a clowder of cats.
items.abstract: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea exposes an ancient piece of the ocean floor and hosts a clowder of cats. The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous, with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building new oceanic crust. In antiquity, Cyprus was known as Ophiousa, or " land of snakes," likely due to its robust population of blunt-nosed vipers. The cape today is still home to the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats, a place where legend says that monks encouraged newly arrived Egyptian cats to hunt snakes. Today, Cyprus has as many cats as people, with more than one million of the feline predators stalking the island.
